passages.source_text: οἱ δὲ ἐπεὶ μὴ πρῶτον τῶν κακῶν ἐπειράθησαν, πρὸς τὴν τῶν ἀγαθῶν δωρεὰν ἀναισθήτως ἔχοντες ὑπὸ τῆς ἀφθόνου τροφῆς καὶ τρυφῆς εἰς ἀχαριστίαν ἐξετρέποντο, ὡς νομίσαι αὐτοὺς μήδ᾽ εἶναι πρόνοιαν, ἐπεὶ μὴ πρότερον καμόντες ἐπὶ δικαιοσύνης· ὡς μισθὸν τὰ ἀγαθὰ εἰλήφεσαν, ἅτε μηδενὸς αὐτῶν ἢ πάθει τινὶ ἢ νόσῳ ἢ ἄλλῃ τινὶ ἀνάγκῃ ὑποπεσόντος, ἵνα (ὡς ἀνθρώποις φίλον ἐστὶν ὑπὸ τῆς κακῆς διαμαρτίας κακωθεῖσιν) ἑαυτοῖς τὸν ἰᾶσθαι δυνάμενον περιβλέψωνται θεόν. ἀλλὰ γὰρ εὐθέως μετὰ τὴν ἐκ τῆς ἀφοβίας καὶ ἀδεοῦς τρυφῆς καταφρόνησιν ὥσπερ ἐξ ἁρμονίας τινὸς ἀκολούθως ἐφηρμοσμένης δικαία τις αὐτοῖς ἀπήντησεν τιμωρία, τὰ μὲν ἀγαθὰ ὡς βλάψαντα ἀπωθοῦσα, τὰ δὲ κακὰ ὡς ὠφελήσαντα ἀντεισφέρουσα.

τῶν γὰρ τὸν οὐρανὸν ἐνοικούντων πνευμάτων οἱ τὴν κατωτάτω χώραν κατοικοῦντες ἄγγελοι, ἀχθεσθέντες ἐπὶ τῇ τῶν ἀνθρώπων εἰς θεὸν ἀχαριστίᾳ αἰτοῦνται εἰς τὸν ἀνθρώπων ἐλθεῖν βίον, ἵνα ὄντως ἄνθρωποι γενόμενοι, ἐπὶ πολιτείᾳ πλείονι τοὺς εἰς αὐτὸν ἀχαριστήσαντας ἐλέγξαντες αὐτόθι τῇ κατ’ ἀξίαν ἕκαστον ὑποβάλωσιν τιμωρίᾳ. ὁπότε οὖν αἰτήσαντες ἔλαβον, πρὸς πᾶσαν ἑαυτοὺς μετέβαλλον φύσιν, ἅτε θειωδεστέρας ὄντες οὐσίας καὶ ῥᾳδίως πρὸς πάντα μετατρέπεσθαι δυνάμενοι. καὶ ἐγένοντο λίθος τίμιος καὶ μαργαρίτης περίβλεπτος πορφύρα τε εἰ τύχοι καλλίστη καὶ χρυσὸς ἔνδοξος καὶ πᾶσα πολυτίμιος ὕλη. καὶ τῶν μὲν εἰς χεῖρας, τῶν δὲ εἰς κόλπον ἐνέπιπτον, καὶ ὑπὸ αὐτῶν ἑκόντες ἐκλέπτοντο, μετεβάλλοντο δὲ καὶ εἰς τετράποδα καὶ εἰς ἑρπετὰ νηκτά τε καὶ πτηνὰ καὶ εἰς πᾶν ὅπερ ἤθελον. ἅτινα καὶ οἱ παρ’ ὑμῖν ποιηταὶ ἀφοβίας αἰτίᾳ ὡς ἔτυχεν ᾄδουσιν, ἐνὶ τοίνυν τὰς πάντων πολλὰς καὶ διαφόρους πράξεις ἀπονέμοντες.

πλὴν ὅτε ταῦτα γενόμενοι τοὺς διαρπάσαντας αὐτοὺς πλεονέκτας ἤλεγξαν καὶ εἰς τὴν ἀνθρώπων φύσιν ἑαυτοὺς μετέβαλον, ἵνα ὁσίως πολιτευσάμενοι καὶ τὸ δυνατὸν τοῦ πολιτεύεσθαι δείξαντες τοὺς ἀχαρίστους εὐθύναις ὑποβάλωσιν, ἐπειδὴ ὄντως τὰ πάντα ἄνθρωποι ἐγίνοντο καὶ τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν ἔσχον τὴν ἀνθρωπίνην, ὑπὸ ταύτης κρατούμενοι εἰς γυναικῶν μίξιν ὤλισθον, αἷς συμπλακέντες καὶ μιασμῷ παγέντες καὶ τῆς πρώτης δυνάμεως παντελῶς κενωθέντες, τὰ ἐκ πυρὸς τραπέντα μέλη εἰς τὸ πρῶτον αὐτῶν τῆς ἰδίας φύσεως ἀμίαντον· μετασυγκρῖναι οὐκ ἐξίσχυσαν. τῷ γὰρ βάρει τῷ ὑπὸ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας εἰς σάρκα τελευτήσαντος αὐτῶν τοῦ πυρός, τὴν ἀσεβοῦσαν ὥδευσαν ὁδὸν κάτω· σαρκὸς γὰρ αὐτοὶ δεσμοῖς πεπεδημένοι κατέσχηνται καὶ ἰσχυρῶς δέδενται, οὗ ἕνεκεν εἰς οὐρανοὺς ἀνελθεῖν οὐκέτι ἐδυνήθησαν.

μετὰ γὰρ συνουσίαν, ὃ τὸ πρῶτον ἐγίνοντο ἀπαιτηθέντες καὶ παρασχεῖν μηκέτι δυνηθέντες, διὰ τὸ ἄλλο τι μετὰ μιασμὸν ἑαυτοὺς ποιῆσαι μὴ δύνασθαι ἀρέσκειν τε ταῖς ἐρωμέναις βουλόμενοι ἀνθ’ ἑαυτῶν τοὺς τῆς γῆς μυελοὺς ὑπέδειξαν, λέγω δὲ τὰ ἐκ μετάλλων ἄνθη, χρυσόν, χαλκόν, ἄργυρον, σίδηρον καὶ τὰ ὅμοια, σὺν τοῖς τιμιωτάτοις ἅπασιν λίθοις. οὖν τούτοις δὲ τοῖς μαγευθεῖσιν λίθοις καὶ τὰς τέχνας τῶν πρὸς ἕκαστα πραγμάτων παρέδοσαν καὶ μαγείας ὑπέδειξαν καὶ ἀστρονομίαν ἐδίδαξαν δυνάμεις τε ῥιζῶν καὶ ὅσα ποτὲ ὑπὸ ἀνθρωπίνης ἐννοίας εὑρεθῆναι ἀδύνατον, ἔτι δὲ χρυσοῦ καὶ ἀργύρου καὶ τῶν ὁμοίων χύσιν τάς τε τῶν ἐσθήτων ποικίλας βαφάς. καὶ πάνθ’ ἁπλῶς ὅσαπερ πρὸς κόσμου καὶ τέρψεώς ἐστι γυναικῶν, τῶν ἐν σαρκὶ δεθέντων δαιμόνων ἐστὶν εὑρέματα.

ἐκ δὲ τῆς νόθου μίξεως αὐτῶν ἄνθρωποι ἐγένοντο νόθοι, πολλῷ γε τῶν ἀνθρώπων κατὰ κορυφὴν μείζους, οὓς οἱ μετὰ ταῦτα γίγαντας ὠνόμασαν, οὐ δρακοντόποδες ὄντες καὶ πρὸς θεὸν πόλεμον ἀράμενοι (ὡς οἱ βλάσφημοι τῶν Ἑλλήνων ᾄδουσιν μῦθοι), ἀλλὰ θηριώδεις τὸν τρόπον καὶ μείζους μὲν ἀνθρώπων τὰ μεγέθη (ἐπείπερ ἐξ ἀγγέλων ἐγένοντο), ἀγγέλων δὲ ἐλάττους (ἐπείπερ ἐκ γυναικῶν γεγέννητο). ὁ οὖν θεὸς εἰδὼς αὐτοὺς πρὸς τὸ θηριῶδες ἐξηγριωμένους καὶ πρὸς τὴν ἑαυτῶν πλησμονὴν τὸν κόσμον οὐκ ἔχοντας αὐτάρκη (πρὸς γὰρ ἀνθρώπων ἀναλογίαν ἐδημιουργήθη καὶ χρῆσιν ἀνθρωπίνην), ἵνα μὴ ἐνδείᾳ τροφῆς ἐπὶ τὴν παρὰ φύσιν τῶν ζῴων βορὰν. τρεπόμενοι ἀνεύθυνοι δοκῶσιν εἶναι, ὡς δι’ ἀνάγκην τοῦτο τετολμηκότες, μάννα αὐτοῖς ὁ παντοδύναμος θεὸς ἐπώμβρισεν ἐκ ποικίλης ἐπιθυμίας, καὶ παντὸς οὗπερ ἐβούλοντο ἀπήλαυον· οἱ δ’ ὑπὸ νόθου φύσεως τῷ καθαρῷ τῆς τροφῆς οὐκ ἀρεσκόμενοι, μόνης τῆς τῶν αἱμάτων γεύσεως ἐγλίχοντα. διὸ καὶ πρῶτοι σαρκῶν ἐγεύσαντο.

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.

passages.text: But because they had not first experienced evils, they were insensible to the gift of good things and, through plentiful nourishment and luxury, were turning toward ingratitude, so that they thought there was no providence at all, since they had received the good things as a reward without first laboring for righteousness. For none of them had fallen under any affliction, sickness, or other necessity, so that—as people are inclined to do when distressed by grievous misfortune—they might look around for the God able to heal them. But in fact, immediately after the contempt born of their fearlessness and carefree luxury, a just punishment met them, as though following from a certain harmoniously ordered sequence: it thrust away the good things as having harmed them and brought in the evils in exchange as having benefited them.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπεὶ μὴ πρότερον καμόντες ἐπὶ δικαιοσύνης· ὡς μισθὸν τὰ ἀγαθὰ εἰλήφεσαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: since they had received the good things as a reward without first laboring for righteousness
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed punctuation and word order favor taking μή with καμόντες: the good things were received without prior righteous labor. A broader scope for μή, “since they had not received the good things as a reward after first laboring for righteousness,” is also grammatically possible and likewise emphasizes that the benefits were unearned.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ τῆς κακῆς διαμαρτίας κακωθεῖσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: when distressed by grievous misfortune
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαμαρτία can denote a failure, reverse, or misfortune; “grievous misfortune” fits the affliction-and-healing context without specifying its nature more narrowly.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὥσπερ ἐξ ἁρμονίας τινὸς ἀκολούθως ἐφηρμοσμένης
lexical_decisions.chosen: as though following from a certain harmoniously ordered sequence
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording depicts punishment as emerging in due succession from an arrangement whose parts have been fitted together harmoniously.

passages.text: For among the spirits inhabiting heaven, the angels dwelling in the lowest region, distressed at humanity’s ingratitude toward God, ask to enter human life, so that, by becoming humans in reality and exposing through their higher way of life those who had been ungrateful to him, they might there and then subject each one to the punishment deserved. When, then, they received what they had asked for, they changed themselves into every kind of nature, since they were of a more divine substance and could readily turn themselves into anything. They became a precious stone, a much-admired pearl, perhaps the most beautiful purple, renowned gold, and every sort of costly material. They fell into the hands of some people and into the laps of others and willingly allowed themselves to be stolen by them. They also changed into four-footed animals, reptiles, swimming creatures, winged creatures, and anything else they wished. Your poets also sing of these things at random because they have no fear, attributing to a single being the many and varied deeds of them all.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν γὰρ τὸν οὐρανὸν ἐνοικούντων πνευμάτων
lexical_decisions.chosen: For among the spirits inhabiting heaven
lexical_decisions.rationale: The initial γάρ explicitly presents the angels’ intervention as an explanation of the punishment introduced in the preceding section.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ πολιτείᾳ πλείονι
lexical_decisions.chosen: through their higher way of life
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολιτεία here denotes conduct or a way of life, and the following section says that the angels intended to demonstrate the possibility of pious conduct. The comparative may alternatively mean “more extensive” rather than “higher.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πορφύρα τε εἰ τύχοι καλλίστη
lexical_decisions.chosen: perhaps the most beautiful purple
lexical_decisions.rationale: πορφύρα may denote purple material or dye, while εἰ τύχοι introduces it as a possible example, literally “if it should happen.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀφοβίας αἰτίᾳ ὡς ἔτυχεν ᾄδουσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: sing of these things at random because they have no fear
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀφοβία literally denotes fearlessness but can imply brazen audacity here; ὡς ἔτυχεν means without careful discrimination, “as it happens” or “at random.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐνὶ τοίνυν τὰς πάντων πολλὰς καὶ διαφόρους πράξεις ἀπονέμοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: attributing to a single being the many and varied deeds of them all
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνί means “to one”; “being” is supplied only to make the otherwise unspecified singular referent intelligible in English.

passages.text: However, when by becoming these things they had exposed as greedy those who seized them, they changed themselves into human nature so that, after living piously and showing that such conduct was possible, they might subject the ungrateful to an accounting. But because they truly became human in every respect and acquired human desire, they were overcome by it and slipped into intercourse with women. Once entangled with them, congealed by defilement, and completely emptied of their original power, they were not strong enough to recombine their limbs, which had been transformed from fire, into the original undefiled state of their own nature. For under the weight of their fire, which through desire had ended in flesh, they traveled the impious road downward. Fettered by bonds of flesh, they have been held down and tightly bound; for this reason they could no longer ascend into the heavens.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπειδὴ ὄντως τὰ πάντα ἄνθρωποι ἐγίνοντο
lexical_decisions.chosen: because they truly became human in every respect
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative τὰ πάντα functions adverbially, indicating complete rather than merely apparent participation in human nature.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μιασμῷ παγέντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: congealed by defilement
lexical_decisions.rationale: παγέντες evokes being fixed, congealed, or solidified. “Made fast by defilement” remains a viable less specific alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ ἐκ πυρὸς τραπέντα μέλη εἰς τὸ πρῶτον αὐτῶν τῆς ἰδίας φύσεως ἀμίαντον· μετασυγκρῖναι οὐκ ἐξίσχυσαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: they were not strong enough to recombine their limbs, which had been transformed from fire, into the original undefiled state of their own nature
lexical_decisions.rationale: The English makes restoration into the original state the unaccomplished result of μετασυγκρῖναι, not the result of the earlier transformation from fire. The supplied high stop before μετασυγκρῖναι makes the attachment visually unusual, so this interpretation remains provisional.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ γὰρ βάρει τῷ ὑπὸ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας εἰς σάρκα τελευτήσαντος αὐτῶν τοῦ πυρός
lexical_decisions.chosen: For under the weight of their fire, which through desire had ended in flesh
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive participle τελευτήσαντος qualifies τοῦ πυρός: their fire had ended in flesh through desire, and its resulting weight bears them downward. The repeated article links the genitive qualification to “weight”; the wording does not make that weight the cause of the transformation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κατέσχηνται
lexical_decisions.chosen: have been held down
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect middle-passive form is understood from κατέχω, “hold” or “restrain.” In context it parallels being fettered and tightly bound.

source_issues.source_quote: εἰς τὸ πρῶτον αὐτῶν τῆς ἰδίας φύσεως ἀμίαντον· μετασυγκρῖναι οὐκ ἐξίσχυσαν.
source_issues.issue: The supplied edition prints a high stop before the delayed infinitive μετασυγκρῖναι. The translation provisionally treats this as an editorial or rhetorical break rather than as a boundary preventing εἰς τὸ πρῶτον αὐτῶν τῆς ἰδίας φύσεως ἀμίαντον from expressing the state into which they could not recombine their limbs. The printed punctuation is verified and is not treated as an OCR defect.

passages.text: For after intercourse, when they were asked for what they had become at first and were no longer able to furnish it—because after defilement they could not turn themselves into anything else—and because they wished to please their beloved women, they showed them, in place of themselves, the marrows of the earth, by which I mean the blooms from mines: gold, copper, silver, iron, and the like, together with all the most precious stones. So to those bewitched by these stones they also handed down the crafts for the operations relating to each one; they disclosed practices of magic, taught astronomy, the powers of roots, and whatever could never be discovered by human thought, and furthermore the casting of gold, silver, and similar materials, as well as the many-colored dyeing of garments. Simply put, everything that serves women’s adornment and pleasure is an invention of the demons bound in flesh.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μετὰ γὰρ συνουσίαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: For after intercourse
lexical_decisions.rationale: The initial γάρ explicitly presents this account as an explanation and elaboration of the loss of transformative power described in the preceding section.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὃ τὸ πρῶτον ἐγίνοντο ἀπαιτηθέντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: when they were asked for what they had become at first
lexical_decisions.rationale: The request concerns their former transformations into precious materials, which they could no longer reproduce after their defilement.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς τῆς γῆς μυελοὺς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the marrows of the earth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The literal anatomical image is retained and immediately explained by the author as metals and precious stones extracted from mines.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὖν τούτοις δὲ τοῖς μαγευθεῖσιν λίθοις
lexical_decisions.chosen: So to those bewitched by these stones
lexical_decisions.rationale: The article with μαγευθεῖσιν is taken substantivally for the recipients, while τούτοις λίθοις identifies the stones by which they were bewitched. A less likely alternative makes all the dative forms one phrase, “these enchanted stones,” but that leaves the dative’s relationship to “handed down” less clear.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰς τέχνας τῶν πρὸς ἕκαστα πραγμάτων
lexical_decisions.chosen: the crafts for the operations relating to each one
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compressed phrase refers to technical arts associated with working or using what had just been listed; “each one” may refer to each material or to each corresponding operation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάνθ’ ἁπλῶς ὅσαπερ πρὸς κόσμου καὶ τέρψεώς ἐστι γυναικῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Simply put, everything that serves women’s adornment and pleasure
lexical_decisions.rationale: κόσμος here means ornament or adornment rather than the physical world.

passages.text: From their illegitimate union came illegitimate human beings, much taller in stature than humans, whom later people called giants. They were not serpent-footed or engaged in war against God, as the blasphemous myths of the Greeks sing, but were beastlike in character—larger than humans in size, since they came from angels, yet smaller than angels, since they had been born from women. God therefore knew that they had grown savage to the point of brutishness and that the world was not sufficient to satisfy them, for it had been created in proportion to human beings and for human use. So that they might not seem free from accountability when, through lack of food, they turned to the unnatural eating of animals, as though they had dared this from necessity, almighty God rained manna down upon them in accordance with their varied desires, and they enjoyed everything they wished for. But because of their illegitimate nature, they were not pleased with the purity of the food; only the taste of blood … . For this reason, too, they were the first to taste flesh.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐκ δὲ τῆς νόθου μίξεως αὐτῶν ἄνθρωποι ἐγένοντο νόθοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: From their illegitimate union came illegitimate human beings
lexical_decisions.rationale: Repeating “illegitimate” preserves the author’s repeated νόθος. “Hybrid” or “mixed” could express their composite origin but would weaken the source’s judgment on the union.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πολλῷ γε τῶν ἀνθρώπων κατὰ κορυφὴν μείζους
lexical_decisions.chosen: much taller in stature than humans
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατὰ κορυφήν concerns height or stature, literally in relation to the head. “Taller by a head” is possible but may impose an exact measurement not required by the phrase.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπείπερ ἐκ γυναικῶν γεγέννητο
lexical_decisions.chosen: since they had been born from women
lexical_decisions.rationale: The English follows the plural giants who are the semantic subject of the surrounding comparison. The supplied γεγέννητο is morphologically third-person singular; it is provisionally construed collectively or as an agreement irregularity rather than silently treated as a printed plural.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀνεύθυνοι δοκῶσιν εἶναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: they might not seem free from accountability
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀνεύθυνος denotes exemption from being called to account, not necessarily moral innocence in a broader sense.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μάννα αὐτοῖς ὁ παντοδύναμος θεὸς ἐπώμβρισεν ἐκ ποικίλης ἐπιθυμίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: almighty God rained manna down upon them in accordance with their varied desires
lexical_decisions.rationale: The following statement that they enjoyed whatever they wanted supports a correspondence between the manna and their varied desires. The phrase ἐκ ποικίλης ἐπιθυμίας may alternatively be causal, “because of” or “in response to their varied appetite,” rather than directly describing the manna’s properties; “in accordance with” leaves that mechanism open.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μόνης τῆς τῶν αἱμάτων γεύσεως ἐγλίχοντα.
lexical_decisions.chosen: only the taste of blood … .
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive phrase is translated, but the printed word ἐγλίχοντα is not: the ellipsis marks unresolved, untranslated wording, not a gap in the printed source. The context and the genitive construction suggest craving the taste of blood, but that meaning requires the conjectural finite form ἐγλίχοντο and cannot be presented as a direct translation of the supplied form.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: σαρκῶν ἐγεύσαντο
lexical_decisions.chosen: taste flesh
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural σαρκῶν refers to animal flesh as food. “Meat” would be idiomatic, but “flesh” retains the source’s bodily image and its connection with the preceding taste of blood.

source_issues.issue: The independently image-checked edition prints the third-person singular γεγέννητο although the surrounding comparison concerns the plural giants. The translation follows that contextual plural subject while disclosing the number irregularity. A collective construal is possible, so this does not by itself prevent a defensible translation; the printed form is not treated as an OCR error.

source_issues.source_quote: ἐπὶ τὴν παρὰ φύσιν τῶν ζῴων βορὰν. τρεπόμενοι
source_issues.issue: The printed period separates τρεπόμενοι from the directional phrase governed by it. The translation provisionally reads the words as one continuing construction while preserving the verified printed punctuation as an editorial feature rather than labeling it an OCR defect.
source_issues.proposed_reading: ἐπὶ τὴν παρὰ φύσιν τῶν ζῴων βορὰν τρεπόμενοι

source_issues.source_quote: μόνης τῆς τῶν αἱμάτων γεύσεως ἐγλίχοντα.
source_issues.issue: The independently image-checked printed word ἐγλίχοντα remains untranslated in the main text and is represented there by an ellipsis; the ellipsis does not indicate a printed gap. As supplied, ἐγλίχοντα does not furnish an established finite plural predicate agreeing with οἱ and does not yield a defensible participial construction in this sentence. The context, the governing genitive, and the plural subject strongly suggest the imperfect middle ἐγλίχοντο, “they craved,” but that is a conjectural correction, not the supplied reading. Because no defensible complete English rendering of the printed construction can presently be given, the passage remains blocked.
source_issues.proposed_reading: μόνης τῆς τῶν αἱμάτων γεύσεως ἐγλίχοντο.

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
